go:39608.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: GA01
go:39608.question:
Out of the following four sentences, select the most suitable sentence with respect to grammar and usage.

  1. I will not leave the place until the minister does not meet me.
  2. I will not leave the place until the minister doesn't meet me.
  3. I will not leave the place until the minister meet me.
  4. I will not leave the place until the minister meets me.

detailed_solution.markdown: "Until" already carries the negative idea, so no "not" after it, and the singular subject "minister" needs "meets".

go:39607.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: GA02
go:39607.question:
A rewording of something written or spoken is a __________.

  1. paraphrase
  2. paradox
  3. paradigm
  4. paraffin

detailed_solution.markdown: A paraphrase restates something in different words. (Paradox = self-contradiction, paradigm = model, paraffin = a wax.)

go:39606.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: GA03
go:39606.question:
Archimedes said, "Give me a lever long enough and a fulcrum on which to place it, and I will move the world."

The sentence above is an example of a ____________ statement.

  1. figurative
  2. collateral
  3. literal
  4. figurine

detailed_solution.markdown: Archimedes did not literally plan to move the world; he used the image to show the power of a lever. That is a figurative statement.

go:39609.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: GA04
go:39609.question:
If 'relftaga' means carefree, 'otaga' means careful and 'fertaga' means careless, which of the following could mean 'aftercare'?

  1. zentaga
  2. tagafer.
  3. tagazen.
  4. relffer.

detailed_solution.markdown: From the words: taga = care, and the modifier comes before taga: relf-taga = free + care (carefree), o-taga = ful + care, fer-taga = less + care. In "aftercare", after comes before care in English, so in this code it comes after taga: taga + (after). Only "tagazen" has that form.

go:39610.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: GA05
go:39610.question:
A cube is built using $64$ cubic blocks of side one unit. After it is built, one cubic block is removed from every corner of the cube. The resulting surface area of the body (in square units) after the removal is ________.

  1. $56$
  2. $64$
  3. $72$
  4. $96$

detailed_solution.markdown:
The 4 $\times$ 4 $\times$ 4 cube has surface area 6 $\times$ 16 = 96.

Removing a corner block removes 3 outer unit faces but exposes 3 new unit faces inside the notch. So the area does not change.

go:39616.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: GA06
go:39616.question:
A shaving set company sells $4$ different types of razors- Elegance, Smooth, Soft and Executive.

Elegance sells at $\text{Rs.} \ 48$, Smooth at $\text{Rs.} \ 63$, Soft at $\text{Rs.} \ 78$ and Executive at $\text{Rs.} \ 173$ per piece. The table below shows the numbers of each razor sold in each quarter of a year.

$$\begin{array}{|c|r|r|r|r|} \hline \textbf{Quarter/Product} & \textbf{Elegance} &\textbf{Smooth} &\textbf{Soft} & \textbf{Executive}\\\hline \text{Q1} & \text{27300} &\text{20009} &\text{17602} &\text{9999}\\\hline \text{Q2} & \text{25222} &\text{19392} & \text{18445}& \text{8942}\\\hline \text{Q3} & \text{28976} &\text{22429} & \text{19544} & \text{10234}\\\hline \text{Q4} &\text{21012} & \text{18229} & \text{16595} & \text{10109}\\\hline \end{array}$$

Which product contributes the greatest fraction to the revenue of the company in that year?

  1. Elegance
  2. Executive
  3. Smooth
  4. Soft

detailed_solution.markdown: Yearly revenue = price $\times$ total units: - Elegance: 48 $\times$ 102510 $\approx$ 49.2 lakh - Smooth: 63 $\times$ 80059 $\approx$ 50.4 lakh - Soft: 78 $\times$ 72186 $\approx$ 56.3 lakh - Executive: 173 $\times$ 39284 $\approx$ 68.0 lakh

go:39613.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: GA07
go:39613.question:
Indian currency notes show the denomination indicated in at least seventeen languages. If this is not an indication of the nation's diversity, nothing else is.

Which of the following can be logically inferred from the above sentences?

  1. India is a country of exactly seventeen languages.
  2. Linguistic pluralism is the only indicator of a nation's diversity.
  3. Indian currency notes have sufficient space for all the Indian languages.
  4. Linguistic pluralism is strong evidence of India's diversity.

detailed_solution.markdown: The sentence says the many languages on the notes are a clear sign of diversity, so linguistic plurality is strong evidence of India's diversity. It does not say exactly 17 languages, or that language is the only indicator.

go:39617.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: GA08
go:39617.question:
Consider the following statements relating to the level of poker play of four players $P,Q,R \ and  \ S$.

  1. $P$ always beats $Q$
  2. $R$ always beats $S$
  3. $S$ loses to $P$ only sometimes.
  4. $R$ always loses to $Q$

Which of the following can be logically inferred from the above statements?

  1. $P$ is likely to beat all the three other players
  2. $S$ is the absolute worst player in the set
  1. (i). only 
  2. (ii) only
  3. (i) and (ii) only'
  4. neither (i) nor (ii)

detailed_solution.markdown:
Checking each statement:

- (i): P beats Q always and S only sometimes; nothing is said about P vs R $\rightarrow$ cannot conclude P beats all three.

- (ii): S loses to R, but S sometimes beats P, so S is not clearly the worst; there is also no information on S vs Q.

go:39611.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: GA09
go:39611.question:
If $f(x) = 2x^{7}+3x-5$, which of the following is a factor of $f(x)$?

  1. $\left(x^{3}+8\right)$
  2. $(x - 1)$
  3. $(2x - 5)$
  4. $(x + 1)$

detailed_solution.markdown:
Factor theorem: $f(1)=2+3-5=0$, so $(x-1)$ is a factor.

(f($-$1) = $-$2 $-$ 3 $-$ 5 $\ne$ 0, so x + 1 is not.)

go:39612.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: GA10
go:39612.question:
In a process, the number of cycles to failure decreases exponentially with an increase in load. At a load of $80$ units, it takes $100$ cycles for failure. When the load is halved, it takes $10000 \ \text{cycles}$ for failure.The load for which the failure will happen in $5000 \ \text{cycles}$ is _____________.

  1. $40.00$
  2. $46.02$
  3. $60.01$
  4. $92.02$

detailed_solution.markdown:
Let cycles $N=Ae^{-kL}$. Halving the load from 80 to 40 multiplies N by 100, so $e^{40k}=100$.

From L = 40 (10000 cycles) to 5000 cycles: $e^{k(L-40)}=2\Rightarrow L-40=\frac{40\ln2}{\ln100}=40\times\frac{0.301}{2}=6.02$

L = 46.02

go:39663.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 1
go:39663.question:
Let $p, q, r, s$ represents the following propositions.

  • $p:x\in\left\{8, 9, 10, 11, 12\right\}$
  • $q:$ $x$ is a composite number.
  • $r:$ $x$ is a perfect square.
  • $s:$ $x$ is a prime number.


The integer $x\geq2$ which satisfies $\neg\left(\left(p\Rightarrow q\right) \wedge \left(\neg r \vee \neg s\right)\right)$ is ____________.

detailed_solution.markdown: $ eg((p\Rightarrow q)\wedge( eg r\vee eg s))\equiv(p\wedge eg q)\vee(r\wedge s)$ - $r\wedge s$ (perfect square and prime) is impossible. - So we need $p\wedge eg q$: x in {8, 9, 10, 11, 12} and not composite. Only 11 qualifies.

go:39636.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 2
go:39636.question:
Let $a_n$ be the number of $n$-bit strings that do NOT contain two consecutive $1's$. Which one of the following is the recurrence relation for $a_n$?

  1. $a_n = a_{n-1}+ 2a_{n-2}$
  2. $a_n = a_{n-1}+ a_{n-2}$
  3. $a_n = 2a_{n-1}+ a_{n-2}$
  4. $a_n = 2a_{n-1}+ 2a_{n-2}$

detailed_solution.markdown:
Look at the first bit of a valid n-bit string:

- starts with 0: the rest is any valid (n $-$ 1)-bit string $\rightarrow$ $a_{n-1}$

- starts with 1: the next bit must be 0, then any valid (n $-$ 2)-bit string $\rightarrow$ $a_{n-2}$

$a_n=a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}$
Put $t=x-4\rightarrow0$: $\lim_{t\to0}\frac{\sin t}{t}=1$.

go:39661.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 04
go:39661.question: A probability density function on the interval $[a, 1]$ is given by $1/x^{2}$ and outside this interval the value of the function is zero. The value of $a$ is _________.

detailed_solution.markdown:
Total probability must be 1:

$\int_a^1\frac{1}{x^2}dx=\left[-\frac1x\right]_a^1=\frac1a-1=1\Rightarrow a=\frac12$

go:39634.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 05
go:39634.question: Two eigenvalues of a $3 \times 3$ real matrix $P$ are $(2+\sqrt {-1})$ and $3$. The determinant of $P$ is _______

detailed_solution.markdown:
A real matrix has complex eigenvalues in conjugate pairs, so $2-i$ is the third eigenvalue.

$\det P=(2+i)(2-i)\times3=(4+1)\times3=15$

go:39629.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 06
go:39629.question:
Consider the Boolean operator # with the following properties :

$x \# 0 = x, x \# 1=\overline{x}, x \# x = 0$ and $x \# \overline{x} = 1.$ Then $x\#y$ is equivalent to 

  1. $x\overline{y}+\overline{x}y$
  2. $x\overline{y}+ \overline{x} \; \overline{y}$
  3. $\overline{x}y+xy$
  4. $xy+\overline{x} \; \overline{y}$

detailed_solution.markdown: $x\#0=x$, $x\#1=\bar x$, $x\#x=0$, $x\#\bar x=1$: these are exactly the properties of XOR. $x\#y=x\bar y+\bar xy$

go:39649.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 07
go:39649.question: The $16\text{-bit}\;2's$ complement representation of an integer is $1111 \quad 1111 \quad 1111 \quad 0101;$ its decimal representation is ____________

detailed_solution.markdown:
The MSB is 1, so the number is negative. Take the 2's complement of 1111 1111 1111 0101:

invert $\rightarrow$ 0000 0000 0000 1010, add 1 $\rightarrow$ 0000 0000 0000 1011 = 11.

go:39670.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 8
go:39670.question: We want to design a synchronous counter that counts the sequence $0-1-0-2-0-3$ and then repeats. The minimum number of $\text{J-K}$ flip-flops required to implement this counter is _____________.

detailed_solution.markdown:
The sequence 0, 1, 0, 2, 0, 3 has 6 steps, and the three 0s are followed by different numbers, so the counter needs 6 different internal states.

6 states need $\lceil\log_2 6\rceil=3$ flip-flops (the output is then decoded from the state).

go:39632.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 09
go:39632.question: A processor can support a maximum memory of $4\;\textsf{GB}$, where the memory is word-addressable (a word consists of two bytes). The size of address bus of the processor is at least _________bits.

detailed_solution.markdown:
4 GB = $2^{32}$ bytes. One word = 2 bytes, so there are $2^{31}$ words.

Word addressable $\rightarrow$ $2^{31}$ addresses $\rightarrow$ 31 address bits.

go:39667.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 10
go:39667.question:
A queue is implemented using an array such that ENQUEUE and DEQUEUE operations are performed efficiently. Which one of the following statements is CORRECT ($n$ refers to the number of items in the queue) ?

  1. Both operations can be performed in $O(1)$ time.
  2. At most one operation can be performed in $O(1)$ time but the worst case time for the operation will be $\Omega (n)$.
  3. The worst case time complexity for both operations will be $\Omega (n)$.
  4. Worst case time complexity for both operations will be $\Omega (\log n)$

detailed_solution.markdown: Use a circular array with front and rear indices: ENQUEUE writes at rear and moves it, DEQUEUE reads at front and moves it (both modulo the array size). No shifting is needed, so both are $O(1)$.

go:39669.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 11
go:39669.question:
Consider the following directed graph:

The number of different topological orderings of the vertices of the graph is _____________.

detailed_solution.markdown:
a must come first and f last. In between, b must come before c, and d before e, but the two chains are independent.

Number of ways to interleave b c with d e = $\binom42=6$.

go:39638.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 12
go:39638.question:
Consider the following "C" program.

void f(int, short);
void main
{
    int i = 100;
    short s = 12;
    short *p = &s;
    ____________;  // call to f
}

 Which one of the following expressions , when placed in the blank above, will NOT result in a type checking error?

  1. $f(s, *s)$
  2. $i = f(i,s)$
  3. $f(i, *s)$
  4. $f(i, *p)$

detailed_solution.concept: Programming in C - Programming In C
detailed_solution.markdown: f takes (int, short) and returns void. - f(s, *s): s is a short, not a pointer, so *s is invalid. - i = f(i, s): f returns void, so it cannot be assigned. - f(i, *s): again *s is invalid. - f(i, *p): i is int, *p is the short s True

go:39660.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 13
go:39660.question:
The worst case running times of Insertion sort , Merge sort and Quick sort, respectively are:

  1. $\Theta (n \log n)$, $\Theta (n \log n)$ and $\Theta(n^2)$
  2. $\Theta (n^2)$, $\Theta (n^2)$ and $\Theta(n \log n)$
  3. $\Theta (n^2)$, $\Theta (n \log n)$ and $\Theta (n \log n)$
  4. $\Theta (n^2)$, $\Theta (n \log n)$ and $\Theta (n^2)$

detailed_solution.markdown:
Checking each statement:

- Insertion sort worst case (reverse sorted): $\Theta(n^2)$

- Merge sort is always $\Theta(n\log n)$

- Quicksort worst case (bad pivots every time): $\Theta(n^2)$

go:39673.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 14
go:39673.question:
Let $G$ be a weighted connected undirected graph with distinct positive edge weights. If every edge weight is increased by the same value, then which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

  • $P$: Minimum spanning tree of $G$ does not change.
  • $Q$: Shortest path between any pair of vertices does not change.
  1. $P$ only
  2. $Q$ only
  3. Neither $P$ nor $Q$
  4. Both $P$ and $Q$

detailed_solution.markdown: Checking each statement: - P: adding the same value to every edge keeps their relative order, so Kruskal picks the same edges $\rightarrow$ the MST does not change $\text{---}$ TRUE. - Q: a path with more edges gains more. E.g. a path 1 + 1 = 2 vs a direct edge 3 becomes 11 + 11 = 22 vs 13 (adding 10) $\rightarrow$ shortest paths can change $\text{---}$ FALSE.

go:39642.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 15
go:39642.question:
Consider the following C program.

# include <stdio.h>
void mystery (int *ptra, int *ptrb) {  
     int *temp; 
     temp = ptrb;  
     ptrb =ptra; 
     ptra = temp; 
} 
int main  { 
    int a = 2016, b=0, c= 4, d = 42; 
    mystery (&a, &b);
    if (a < c) 
          mystery (&c, &a); 
    mystery (&a, &d); 
    printf("%d\n", a); 
}

The output of the program is _________.

detailed_solution.concept: Programming in C - Programming In C
detailed_solution.markdown: mystery only swaps its local pointer copies (ptra, ptrb); it never changes *ptra or *ptrb. So a, b, c, d in main never change. a is still 2016.

go:39640.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 16
go:39640.question:
Which of the following languages is generated by the given grammar?

$$S \rightarrow aS \mid bS \mid \varepsilon$$

  1. $\{ a^nb^m \mid n,m \geq 0\}$
  2. $\{ w \in \{ a,b\}^* \mid w\text{ has equal number of a's and b's}\}$
  3. $\{a^n \mid n \geq 0 \} \cup \{b^n \mid n \geq 0\} \cup \{a^n b^n \mid n \geq 0\}$
  4. $\{ a,b\}^*$

detailed_solution.concept: Theory of Computation - Context Free Language
detailed_solution.markdown: $S\rightarrow aS\mid bS\mid\varepsilon$ adds any a or b at each step, in any order and any number of times, so it generates every string over {a, b}, including $\varepsilon$.

go:39651.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 17
go:39651.question:
Which of the following decision problems are undecidable?

  1. Given NFAs $N_1$ and $N_2$ , is $L(N_1) \cap L(N_2) = \Phi$
  2. Given a CFG $G = (N,\Sigma,P,S)$ and a string  $x \in \Sigma^{*}$, does  $x \in L(G)$} ?
  3. Given CFGs  $G_1$ and $G_2$, is $L (G_1) = L(G_2)$?
  4. Given a TM $M$, is $L(M)=\Phi$ ?
  1. I and IV only
  2. II and III only 
  3. III and IV only
  4. II and IV only

detailed_solution.markdown: Checking each statement: - I: NFA intersection emptiness: build the product automaton and check reachability $\rightarrow$ decidable. - II: CFG membership: CYK algorithm $\rightarrow$ decidable. - III: equivalence of two CFGs $\rightarrow$ undecidable. - IV: emptiness of a TM's language (Rice) $\rightarrow$ undecidable.

go:39647.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 18
go:39647.question:
Which one of the following regular expressions represents the language: the set of all binary strings having two consecutive $0$'s and two consecutive $1$'s?

  1. $(0+1 )^ *0011 (0+1)^* +(0+1)^*1100(0+1)^*$
  2. $(0+1)^* (00(0+1)^*11+11(0+1)^*00)(0+1)^*$
  3. $(0+1)^*00(0+1)^* + (0+1)^*11 (0+1)^*$
  4. $00(0+1)^*11 +11(0+1)^*00$

detailed_solution.markdown:
The string must contain "00" somewhere and "11" somewhere, in either order:

$(0+1)^*\big(00(0+1)^*11+11(0+1)^*00\big)(0+1)^*$ True

- Option 1 forces 00 and 11 to be adjacent (0011 or 1100).

- Option 3 needs only one of them.

- Option 4 forces them at the very start and end.

go:39675.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 19
go:39675.question:
Consider the following code segment.

x = u - t;
y = x * v; 
x = y + w;
y = t - z; 
y = x * y;

The minimum number of total variables required to convert the above code segment to static single assignment form is __________.

detailed_solution.markdown:
In SSA form every assignment gets a new variable:

$x_1=u-t;\ y_1=x_1v;\ x_2=y_1+w;\ y_2=t-z;\ y_3=x_2y_2$

New variables: $x_1,y_1,x_2,y_2,y_3$ (5), plus the inputs u, t, v, w, z (5).

Total = 10

go:39655.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 20
go:39655.question:
Consider an arbitrary set of CPU-bound processes with unequal CPU burst lengths submitted at the same time to a computer system. Which one of the following process scheduling algorithms would minimize the average waiting time in the ready queue?

  1. Shortest remaining time first
  2. Round-robin with the time quantum less than the shortest CPU burst 
  3. Uniform random
  4. Highest priority first with priority proportional to CPU burst length

detailed_solution.markdown: All processes arrive together, so shortest remaining time first behaves like SJF, which is optimal for average waiting time. Round robin, random order or "long jobs first" make short jobs wait longer.

go:39637.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 21
go:39637.question:
Which of the following is NOT a superkey in a relational schema with attributes $V,W,X,Y,Z$ and primary key $V\;Y$?

  1. $VXYZ$
  2. $VWXZ$
  3. $VWXY$
  4. $VWXYZ$

detailed_solution.markdown: A superkey must contain the whole primary key {V, Y}. VWXZ has V but no Y $\rightarrow$ not a superkey. The others all contain both V and Y.

go:39644.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 22
go:39644.question:
Which one of the following is NOT a part of the ACID properties of database transactions?

  1. Atomicity
  2. Consistency
  3. Isolation
  4. Deadlock-freedom

detailed_solution.markdown: ACID = Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability. Deadlock-freedom is not one of them.

go:39646.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 23
go:39646.question:
A database of research articles in a journal uses the following schema.

$\text{(VOLUME, NUMBER, STARTPAGE, ENDPAGE, TITLE, YEAR, PRICE)}$

The primary key is '$\text{(VOLUME, NUMBER, STARTPAGE, ENDPAGE)}$

and the following functional dependencies exist in the schema.

$\begin{align*}&(\text{VOLUME , NUMBER, STARTPAGE, ENDPAGE}) & \rightarrow \text{TITLE} \\ &(\text{VOLUME, NUMBER}) & \rightarrow  \text{ YEAR} \\ &(\text{VOLUME, NUMBER, STARTPAGE, ENDPAGE})        &\rightarrow  \text{PRICE} \end{align*}$

The database is redesigned to use the following schemas

$(\text{VOLUME, NUMBER, STARTPAGE, ENDPAGE, TITLE, PRICE}) \\ \text{(VOLUME, NUMBER, YEAR})$

Which is the weakest normal form that the new database satisfies, but the old one does not?

  1. $\text{1NF}$
  2. $\text{2NF}$
  3. $\text{3NF}$
  4. $\text{BCNF}$

detailed_solution.markdown: Old schema: key (VOLUME, NUMBER, STARTPAGE, ENDPAGE), and (VOLUME, NUMBER) $\rightarrow$ YEAR is a partial dependency (part of the key determines a non-key attribute) $\rightarrow$ only 1NF. New schemas: YEAR moves to (VOLUME, NUMBER, YEAR), so the partial dependency is gone $\rightarrow$ 2NF (in fact both are in BCNF). The weakest form the new one satisfies but the old one does not is 2NF.

go:39639.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 24
go:39639.question:
Which one of the following protocols is NOT used to resolve one form of address to another one?

  1. $\textsf{DNS}$
  2. $\textsf{ARP}$
  3. $\textsf{DHCP}$
  4. $\textsf{RARP}$

detailed_solution.markdown: Checking each statement: - DNS: hostname $\rightarrow$ IP - ARP: IP $\rightarrow$ MAC - RARP: MAC $\rightarrow$ IP - DHCP assigns IP configuration to hosts; it does not translate one address form into another.

go:39628.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 25
go:39628.question:
Which of the following is/are example(s) of stateful application layer protocol?

  1. $\textsf{HTTP}$
  2. $\textsf{FTP}$
  3. $\textsf{TCP}$
  4. $\textsf{POP3}$
  1. $\text{(i)}$ and $\text{(ii)}$ only
  2. $\text{(ii)}$ and $\text{(iii)}$ only
  3. $\text{(ii)}$ and $\text{(iv)}$ only
  4. $\text{(iv)}$ only

detailed_solution.markdown:
Checking each statement:

- HTTP is stateless (each request is independent).

- FTP keeps session state (login, current directory) $\rightarrow$ stateful.

- TCP is a transport protocol, not application layer.

- POP3 keeps session state (authorization, transaction states) $\rightarrow$ stateful.

$(x^3+x^4+\cdots)^3=x^9(1+x+x^2+\cdots)^3=x^9(1-x)^{-3}$

We need the coefficient of $x^3$ in $(1-x)^{-3}$: $\binom{3+2}{2}=10$.

go:39714.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 27
go:39714.question: Consider the recurrence relation $a_1 =8 , a_n =6n^2 +2n+a_{n-1}$. Let  $a_{99}=K\times 10^4$. The value of $K$ is __________.

go:39717.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 28
go:39717.question:
A function $f: \Bbb{N^+} \rightarrow \Bbb{N^+}$ , defined on the set of positive integers $\Bbb{N^+}$, satisfies the following properties:

                    $f(n)=f(n/2)$   if $n$ is even

                    $f(n)=f(n+5)$  if $n$ is odd

Let $R=\{ i \mid \exists{j} : f(j)=i \}$ be the set of distinct values that $f$ takes. The maximum possible size of $R$ is ___________.

detailed_solution.markdown:
Both rules keep a number inside its class:

- If n is a multiple of 5, n/2 (when even) and n + 5 are still multiples of 5.

- If n is not a multiple of 5, neither are n/2 and n + 5.

Within each class all values are linked (e.g. 1 $\rightarrow$ 6 $\rightarrow$ 3 $\rightarrow$ 8 $\rightarrow$ 4 $\rightarrow$ 2 $\rightarrow$ 1, and 5 $\rightarrow$ 10 $\rightarrow$ 5), so f can take at most one value per class: at most 2 values.

go:39709.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 29
go:39709.question:
Consider the following experiment.

Step 1. Flip a fair coin twice.

Step 2. If the outcomes are (TAILS, HEADS) then output $Y$ and stop.

Step 3. If the outcomes are either (HEADS, HEADS) or (HEADS, TAILS), then output $N$ and stop.

Step 4. If the outcomes are (TAILS, TAILS), then go to Step $1.$

The probability that the output of the experiment is $Y$ is (up to two decimal places)

detailed_solution.markdown:
In each round of two flips: Y with probability 1/4 (TH), N with 1/2 (HH or HT), repeat with 1/4 (TT).

$P(Y)=\frac{1/4}{1/4+1/2}=\frac13\approx0.33$

go:39722.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 30
go:39722.question:
Consider the two cascade $2$ to $1$ multiplexers as shown in the figure .

    

The minimal sum of products form of the output $X$ is 

  1. $\overline{P} \ \overline {Q}+PQR$
  2. $\overline{P} \ {Q}+QR$
  3. $PQ +\overline{P} \ \overline{Q}R$
  4. $\overline{Q} \ \overline{R} + PQR$

detailed_solution.markdown:
First mux (select P): output = R if P = 1, else 0 $\rightarrow$ PR.

Second mux (select Q): X = PR if Q = 1, else $\bar R$.

$X=\bar Q\bar R+QPR$

go:39698.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 31
go:39698.question: The size of the data count register of a $\text{DMA}$ controller is $16\;\text{bits}$. The processor needs to transfer a file of $29,154$ kilobytes from disk to main memory. The memory is byte addressable. The minimum number of times the $\text{DMA}$ controller needs to get the control of the system bus from the processor to transfer the file from the disk to main memory is _________.

detailed_solution.markdown:
A 16-bit count register lets the DMA move at most $2^{16}$ bytes = 64 KB each time it takes the bus.

$\lceil29154/64\rceil=\lceil455.5\rceil=456$

go:39691.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 32
go:39691.question: The stage delays in a $4$-stage pipeline are $800, 500, 400$ and $300$ picoseconds. The first stage (with delay $800$ picoseconds) is replaced with a functionality equivalent design involving two stages with respective delays $600$ and $350$ picoseconds. The throughput increase of the pipeline is ___________ percent.

detailed_solution.markdown:
Throughput is 1 / (slowest stage).

- Before: max delay 800 ps.

- After: stages 600, 350, 500, 400, 300 $\rightarrow$ max 600 ps.

Increase $=\frac{1/600-1/800}{1/800}=\frac{800}{600}-1=33.3\%$

go:39688.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 33
go:39688.question:
Consider a carry look ahead adder for adding two $n$-bit integers, built using gates of fan-in at most two. The time to perform addition using this adder is

  1. $\Theta (1)$
  2. $\Theta (\log(n))$
  3. $\Theta (\sqrt{n})$
  4. $\Theta (n)$)

detailed_solution.markdown: Carry lookahead computes all carries from the generate/propagate signals. With gates of fan-in 2, combining n signals needs a tree of depth $\log_2 n$.

go:39704.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 34
go:39704.question:
The following function computes the maximum value contained in an integer array $P[ \ ]$ of size $n$ $(n>=1)$.                  

int max (int *p,int n) {
    int a = 0, b=n-1;
    
    while (__________) {
        if (p[a]<= p[b]) {a = a+1;}
        else             {b = b-1;}
    }
    return p[a];
}

The missing loop condition is:

  1.  $a\ \ != n$ 
  2.  $b\ \ != 0$ 
  3.  $b>(a+1)$ 
  4.  $b\ \ != a$

detailed_solution.concept: Programming in C - Programming In C
detailed_solution.markdown:
Two pointers start at the ends; each step discards the smaller of p[a] and p[b] (the maximum is never discarded). The loop must stop when only one candidate is left, i.e. when a and b meet.

Loop condition: b != a.

go:39730.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 35
go:39730.question:
What will be the output of the following $C$ program?

void count (int n) {
    static int d=1;
    
    printf ("%d",n);
    printf ("%d",d);
    d++;
    if (n>1) count (n-1);
    printf ("%d",d);
    
    
}

void main{
    count (3);
}
  1. $3 \ 1 \ 2 \ 2 \ 1 \ 3  \ 4 \ 4 \ 4$ 
  2.  $3 \ 1 \ 2  \ 1  \ 1 \ 1 \ 2 \ 2 \ 2$ 
  3.  $3 \ 1  \ 2 \ 2 \ 1 \ 3 \ 4$ 
  4.  $3 \ 1 \ 2  \ 1  \ 1  \ 1  \ 2$

detailed_solution.concept: Programming in C - Programming In C
detailed_solution.markdown:
d is static (one copy, starts at 1).

- count(3): prints 3, 1; d = 2; calls count(2)

- count(2): prints 2, 2; d = 3; calls count(1)

- count(1): prints 1, 3; d = 4; prints 4

- back in count(2): prints 4; back in count(3): prints 4

Output: 3 1 2 2 1 3 4 4 4

go:39701.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 36
go:39701.question:
What will be the output of the following pseudo-code when parameters are passed by reference and dynamic scoping is assumed?                

a = 3;
void n(x) { x = x * a; print (x); }
void m(y) { a = 1 ; a = y - a;  n(a); print (a); }
void main  { m(a); }
  1. $6,2$ 
  2.  $6,6$ 
  3.  $4,2$ 
  4.  $4,4$

detailed_solution.markdown: Read "a = 1" in m as declaring a local a of m. y refers to the global a (= 3). - m: local a = 1, then a = y $-$ a = 3 $-$ 1 = 2. - n(a): x refers to m's local a. With dynamic scoping, the a inside n is also m's a (the most recent active a). x = x $\times$ a = 2 $\times$ 2 = 4, and since x is that same a, a becomes 4. Prints 4. - Back in m: print(a) prints 4.

go:39706.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 37
go:39706.question:
An operator $delete(i)$ for a binary heap data structure is to be designed to delete the item in the $i$-th  node. Assume that the heap is implemented in an array and $i$ refers to the $i$-th index of the array. If the heap tree has depth $d$ (number of edges on the path from the root to the farthest leaf ), then what is the time complexity to re-fix the heap efficiently after the removal of the element?

  1.  $O(1)$ 
  2.  $O(d)$ but not $O(1)$ 
  3.  $O(2^d)$ but not $O(d)$ 
  4.  $O(d \ 2^d)$ but not $O(2^d)$

detailed_solution.markdown: To delete node i: move the last element into position i, then either sift it up or down. Either way it moves along one root-to-leaf path, at most d levels $\rightarrow$ $O(d)$. It can take that long, so it is not $O(1)$.

go:39731.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 38
go:39731.question:
Consider the weighted undirected graph with $4$ vertices, where the weight of edge $\{i,j\}$ is given by the entry $W_{ij}$ in the matrix $W$.

 W=$\begin{bmatrix} 0&2 &8 &5 \\ 2&0 &5 &8 \\ 8&5 &0 &x \\ 5& 8 &x &0 \end{bmatrix}$

The largest possible integer value of $x$, for which at least one shortest path between some pair of vertices will contain the edge with weight $x$ is ___________.

detailed_solution.markdown:
Without edge {3, 4}, the shortest path from 3 to 4 is 3-2-1-4 = 5 + 2 + 5 = 12.

The edge of weight x lies on a shortest path (at least one, possibly tied) only if $x\le12$. The largest integer is 12.

go:39725.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 39
go:39725.question: Let $G$ be a complete undirected graph on $4$ vertices, having $6$ edges with weights being $1, 2, 3,  4, 5,$ and $6$. The maximum possible weight that a minimum weight spanning tree of $G$ can have is __________

detailed_solution.markdown:
An MST of 4 vertices has 3 edges; edges 1 and 2 are always taken (two edges cannot form a cycle).

To make the third edge as heavy as possible, put edges 1, 2, 3 in a triangle, so 3 is rejected. The 4th vertex must then be joined by the next lightest edge, 4.

Maximum MST weight = 1 + 2 + 4 = 7

go:39727.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 40
go:39727.question:
$G=(V, E)$ is an undirected simple graph in which each edge has a distinct weight, and $e$ is a particular edge of $G$. Which of the following statements about the minimum spanning trees $(MSTs)$ of $G$ is/are TRUE?

  1. If $e$ is the lightest edge of some cycle in $G$, then every MST of $G$ includes $e$.
  2. If $e$ is the heaviest edge of some cycle in $G$, then every MST of $G$ excludes $e$.
  1. I only.
  2. II only.
  3. Both I and II.
  4. Neither I nor II.

detailed_solution.markdown: Checking each statement: - I: the lightest edge of one cycle can still be the heaviest edge of another cycle and be excluded $\text{---}$ FALSE. - II: cycle property: with distinct weights, the heaviest edge of any cycle is in no MST $\text{---}$ TRUE.

go:39684.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 41
go:39684.question:
Let $Q$ denote a queue containing sixteen numbers and $S$ be an empty stack. $Head(Q)$ returns the element at the head of the queue $Q$ without removing it from $Q$. Similarly $Top(S)$ returns the element at the top of $S$ without removing it from $S$. Consider the algorithm given below.

while Q is not Empty do 
  if S is Empty OR Top(S) ≤ Head (Q) then 
     x:= Dequeue (Q); 
     Push (S, x); 
  else  
     x:= Pop(S); 
     Enqueue (Q, x);
  end
 end

The maximum possible number of iterations of the while loop in the algorithm is _______.

detailed_solution.markdown:
The loop keeps the stack in sorted order, sending larger stack tops back to the queue. The worst case is when the queue is in decreasing order: every element has to be cycled between the stack and the queue many times.

For n elements the worst case is $n^2$ iterations (check n = 2 with queue [2, 1]: 4 iterations). For n = 16: $16^2=256$.

go:39705.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 42
go:39705.question:
Consider the following context-free grammars;

$G_1 : S \to aS \mid B, B \to b \mid bB$

$G_2 : S \to aA \mid bB, A \to aA \mid B \mid \varepsilon,B \to bB \mid \varepsilon$

Which one of the following pairs of languages is generated by $G_1$ and $G_2$ ,respectively?

  1.  $\{ a^mb^n \mid m > 0 \text{ or } n >0\}$ and $\{ a^mb^n \mid m > 0 \text{ and } n >0\}$ 
  2.  $\{ a^mb^n \mid m > 0 \text{ and } n >0\}$ and $\{ a^mb^n \mid m > 0 \text{ or } n\geq0\}$
  3.  $\{ a^mb^n \mid m \geq 0 \text{ or } n >0\}$ and $\{ a^mb^n \mid m > 0\text{ and } n>0\}$
  4.  $\{ a^mb^n \mid m \geq 0 \text{ and } n >0\}$ and $\{ a^mb^n \mid m > 0 \text{ or } n>0\}$

detailed_solution.concept: Theory of Computation - Context Free Language
detailed_solution.markdown:
Checking each statement:

- G1: $S\rightarrow aS\mid B$, $B\rightarrow b\mid bB$ gives $a^*b^+$ $\rightarrow$ $\{a^mb^n\mid m\ge0,\ n \gt 0\}$.

- G2: aA gives $a^+b^*$ and bB gives $b^+$ $\rightarrow$ $\{a^mb^n\mid m \gt 0\text{ or }n \gt 0\}$.

go:39732.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 43
go:39732.question:
Consider the transition diagram of a PDA given below with input alphabet $\Sigma=\{a,b\}$ and stack alphabet $\Gamma = \{X,Z\}$. $Z$ is the initial stack symbol. Let $L$ denote the language accepted by the PDA

Which one of the following is TRUE? 

  1. $L =\{a^nb^n\mid n \geq0 \}$ and is not accepted by any finite automata 
  2. $L =\{a^n\mid n \geq0 \} \cup \{a^nb^n \mid n \geq 0\}$ and is not accepted by any deterministic PDA 
  3. $L$ is not accepted by any Turing machine that halts on every input 
  4. $L =\{a^n\mid n \geq0 \} \cup \{a^nb^n \mid n \geq 0\}$ and is deterministic context-free

detailed_solution.markdown: The PDA pushes an X for every a in the start state (which is final), then pops one X per b, and accepts when only Z is left. So $L=\{a^n\mid n\ge0\}\cup\{a^nb^n\mid n\ge1\}$, and every move is deterministic $\rightarrow$ L is a deterministic CFL.

go:39721.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 44
go:39721.question:
Let $X$ be a recursive language and $Y$ be a recursively enumerable but not recursive language. Let $W$  and $Z$ be two languages such that $\overline{Y}$ reduces to $W$, and $Z$ reduces to $\overline{X}$ (reduction means the standard many-one reduction). Which one of the following statements is TRUE?

  1. $W$ can be recursively enumerable and $Z$ is recursive.
  2. $W$ can be recursive and $Z$ is recursively enumerable.
  3. $W$ is not recursively enumerable and $Z$ is recursive.
  4. $W$ is not recursively enumerable and $Z$ is not recursive.

detailed_solution.concept: Theory of Computation - Recursive and Recursively Enumerable Languages
detailed_solution.markdown: Checking each statement: - Y is RE but not recursive, so $\bar Y$ is not RE. Since $\bar Y$ reduces to W, W cannot be RE (otherwise $\bar Y$ would be). - X is recursive, so $\bar X$ is recursive. Z reduces to $\bar X$, so Z is recursive.

go:39697.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 45
go:39697.question:
The attribute of three arithmetic operators in some programming language are given below.
$$\begin{array}{|c|l|}\hline \textbf{OPERATOR}  &  \textbf{PRECEDENCE} & \textbf{ASSOCIATIVITY} & \textbf{ARITY} \\\hline  \text{$+$} & \text{High} & \text{Left} & \text{Binary} \\\hline  \text{$-$} & \text{Medium} & \text{Right} & \text{Binary} \\\hline  \text{$*$} & \text{Low} & \text{Left} & \text{Binary} \\\hline \end{array}$$
The value of the expression $2-5+1-7*3$ in this language is ________.

detailed_solution.markdown:
Precedence: + (highest) $\gt$ $-$ $\gt$ * (lowest). So * is applied last:

$(2-5+1-7)*3$

Inside: + first, 5 + 1 = 6 $\rightarrow$ 2 $-$ 6 $-$ 7. $-$ is right associative: $2-(6-7)=2-(-1)=3$.

$3*3=9$

go:39700.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 46
go:39700.question:
Consider the following Syntax Directed Translation Scheme $( SDTS )$, with non-terminals $\{S,A \}$ and terminals $\{a,b \}$.

          $S \to aA  \quad \{\text{print }1\}$

          $S \to a    \quad   \{\text{print }2\}$

          $A \to Sb  \quad \{\text{print }3\}$

Using the above $SDTS$ , the output printed by a bottom-up parser, for the input $aab$ is:

  1.  $1 \ 3 \ 2 $ 
  2.  $2 \ 2 \ 3  $ 
  3.  $2 \ 3 \ 1 $ 
  4.  syntax error

detailed_solution.markdown: Parse aab bottom-up: 1. The second a is reduced by $S\rightarrow a$ $\rightarrow$ prints 2 2. S b is reduced by $A\rightarrow Sb$ $\rightarrow$ prints 3 3. a A is reduced by $S\rightarrow aA$ $\rightarrow$ prints 1

go:39690.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 47
go:39690.question: Consider a computer system with $40$-bit virtual addressing and page size of sixteen kilobytes. If the computer system has a one-level page table per process and each page table entry requires $48$ bits, then the size of the per-process page table is __________ megabytes.

detailed_solution.markdown:
Entries = $\frac{2^{40}}{2^{14}}=2^{26}$. Each entry = 48 bits = 6 bytes.

Size $=2^{26}\times6=6\times64\text{ MB}=384$ MB

go:39716.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 48
go:39716.question: Cylinder a disk queue with requests for $I/O$ to blocks on cylinders $47, 38, 121, 191, 87, 11, 92, 10.$ The C-LOOK scheduling algorithm is used. The head is initially at cylinder number $63$, moving towards larger cylinder numbers on its servicing pass. The cylinders are numbered from $0$ to $199$. The total head movement (in number of cylinders) incurred while servicing these requests is__________.

detailed_solution.markdown:
C-LOOK from 63 going up: 87, 92, 121, 191 (movement 191 $-$ 63 = 128), then jump to the lowest request 10 (191 $-$ 10 = 181), then 11, 38, 47 (47 $-$ 10 = 37).

Total = 128 + 181 + 37 = 346

go:39711.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 49
go:39711.question: Consider a computer system with ten physical page frames. The system is provided with an access sequence $(a_{1}, a_{2},....,a_{20}, a_{1}, a_{2},...a_{20})$, where each $a_{i}$ is a distinct virtual page number. The difference in the number of page faults between the last-in-first-out page replacement policy and the optimal page replacement policy is_________.

detailed_solution.markdown: LIFO: the first pass gives 20 faults; a1-a9 stay in memory and the 10th frame keeps getting replaced (ends with a20). Second pass: a1-a9 hit, a10-a20 fault (11). Total 31. Optimal: 20 faults in the first pass and only 10 in the second (it keeps 10 of the pages needed next). Total 30. Difference = 31 $-$ 30 = 1

go:39719.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 50
go:39719.question:
Consider the following proposed solution for the critical section problem. There are $n$ processes : $P_0....P_{n-1}$. In the code, function $\text{pmax}$ returns an integer not smaller than any of its arguments .For all $i,t[i]$ is initialized to zero.

Code for $P_i$;

do {
    c[i]=1; t[i]= pmax (t[0],....,t[n-1])+1; c[i]=0;
    for every j != i in {0,....,n-1} {
        while (c[j]); 
        while (t[j] != 0 && t[j] <=t[i]);
    }
    Critical Section;
    t[i]=0;
    
    Remainder Section;
    
}  while (true);

Which of the following is TRUE about the above solution?

  1. At most one process can be in the critical section at any time
  2. The bounded wait condition is satisfied
  3. The progress condition is satisfied
  4. It cannot cause a deadlock

detailed_solution.markdown: This is a bakery-style algorithm: a process enters only after every other process with a smaller (non-zero) ticket has finished, so mutual exclusion holds. But two processes can pick the same ticket (pmax is not atomic). Then each waits for the other (t[j] $\le$ t[i] holds both ways) $\rightarrow$ deadlock, so progress and bounded waiting also fail.

go:39703.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 51
go:39703.question:
Consider the following two phase locking protocol. Suppose a transaction $T$ accesses (for read or write operations), a certain set of objects $\{O_1,\ldots,O_k \}$. This is done in the following manner:

  • $\text{Step 1}$. $T$ acquires exclusive locks to $O_1,\ldots,O_k$ in increasing order of their addresses.
  • $\text{Step 2}$. The required operations are performed .
  • $\text{Step 3}$. All locks are released

This protocol will

  1.  guarantee serializability and  deadlock-freedom 
  2.  guarantee neither serializability nor deadlock-freedom 
  3.  guarantee serializability but not deadlock-freedom  
  4.  guarantee deadlock-freedom but not serializability.

detailed_solution.markdown: All locks are taken before any operation and released only at the end $\rightarrow$ a two-phase locking schedule $\rightarrow$ serializable. Locks are always requested in increasing address order, so no circular wait can form $\rightarrow$ deadlock-free.

go:39694.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 52
go:39694.question:
Consider that $B$ wants to send a message $m$ that is digitally signed to $A$. Let the pair of private and public keys for $A$ and $B$ be denoted by ${K_{x}}^-$ and ${K_{x}}^+$ for $x=A, B$, respectively. Let $K_{x}(m)$ represent the operation of encrypting $m$ with a key $K_{x}$ and $H(m)$ represent the message digest. Which one of the following indicates the CORRECT way of sending the message $m$ along with the digital signature to $A$?

  1. $\left\{m, {K_{B}}^+(H(m))\right\}$
  2. $\left\{m, {K_{B}}^-(H(m))\right\}$
  3. $\left\{m, {K_{A}}^-(H(m))\right\}$
  4. $\left\{m, {K_{A}}^+(m)\right\}$

detailed_solution.markdown: B signs by encrypting the digest with B's private key: $K_B^-(H(m))$. A checks it with B's public key $K_B^+$ and compares with H(m).

go:39712.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 53
go:39712.question:
An IP datagram of size $1000$ $\text{bytes }$arrives at a router. The router has to forward this packet on a link whose MTU (maximum transmission unit) is $100$ $\text{bytes }$. Assume that the size of the IP header is $20$ $\text{bytes }.$

The number of fragments that the IP datagram will be divided into for transmission is________.

detailed_solution.markdown:
Data = 1000 $-$ 20 = 980 bytes. Per fragment: 100 $-$ 20 = 80 bytes of data (already a multiple of 8).

Fragments = $\lceil980/80\rceil=\lceil12.25\rceil=13$

go:39720.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 54
go:39720.question: For a host machine that uses the token bucket algorithm for congestion control, the token bucket has a capacity of $1$ $\text{megabyte}$ and the maximum output rate is $20$ $\text{megabytes}$ per $\text{second}$. Tokens arrive at a rate to sustain output at a rate of $10$ $\text{megabytes}$ per $\text{second}$. The token bucket is currently full and the machine needs to send $12$ $\text{megabytes}$ of data. The minimum time required to transmit the data is _____________ $\text{seconds}$.

detailed_solution.markdown:
Bucket starts full (1 MB). While it drains, the host sends at 20 MB/s while tokens arrive at 10 MB/s:

$20t=1+10t\Rightarrow t=0.1$ s, sending 2 MB.

The remaining 10 MB go at 10 MB/s = 1 s.

Total = 0.1 + 1 = 1.1 s

go:39696.title: GATE CSE 2016 Set 1 | Question: 55
go:39696.question:
A sender uses the Stop-and-Wait $\text{ARQ}$ protocol for reliable transmission of frames. Frames are of size $1000$ bytes and the transmission rate at the sender is $80\;\textsf{Kbps} (1\textsf{Kbps} = 1000\;\text{ bits/second}).$  Size of an acknowledgment is $100$ bytes and the transmission rate at the receiver is $8\;\textsf{Kbps.}$ The one-way propagation delay is $100$ milliseconds.

Assuming no frame is lost, the sender throughput is ________ bytes/ second.

detailed_solution.markdown:
Checking each statement:

- Frame transmission: 8000 bits / 80 Kbps = 0.1 s

- ACK transmission: 800 bits / 8 Kbps = 0.1 s

- Propagation: 0.1 s each way

One frame every 0.1 + 0.1 + 0.1 + 0.1 = 0.4 s $\rightarrow$ throughput = 1000 / 0.4 = 2500 bytes/s
